title: UFOs: Generals, Pilots, and Government Officials Go on the Record
author: Leslie Kean
vetoReason: The book's residual-unexplained-case argument relies on discounting ordinary explanations and treating witness rank as unusually strong evidence. Robert Sheaffer's specific critique identifies omitted competing analyses of central cases and contrary testimony from Hynek on pilot reliability. These objections concern the evidential selection underlying the central argument, not simply the possibility of extraterrestrial life.
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage. Nonfiction investigation, not fiction or religious doctrine. Publisher-reproduced praise from Kaku, Lane and other scientists was considered. Kean's 2010 reply says she concentrates on the thoroughly investigated residual five percent and seeks investigation rather than proof of extraterrestrial origin. That defense does not resolve the documented problem of omitted alternatives. V9 does not assume every sighting has been explained. No thematic deduction: anomalous observations, not military doctrine, are central. Not selected.
notes: Selective treatment of contrary case analysis weakens the central inference.
Connects observation, aviation and government response, with limited broader integration.
Some lessons about reporting anomalous observations, but unsafe evidential heuristics.
Unresolved reports do not establish the cause or operating mechanism.
D=6, moderate confidence from Sheaffer's detailed review, publisher material and readers. Cases supply different observations, though repeated credentials add less learning.
A historical record of claims, but central conclusions remain disputed.
Aviation and scientific evidence partly fit; little engineering explanation.
Experienced reporter with high-status endorsers, countered by specific case investigators.
Readable first-person cases and clear organization.
Clarity is stronger than calibration of claims.

title: Ending Aging: The Rejuvenation Breakthroughs That Could Reverse Human Aging in Our Lifetime
author: Aubrey de Grey and Michael Rae
vetoReason: The central promise requires a proposed set of damage-repair interventions to be sufficiently complete and jointly feasible to produce repeated rejuvenation. Warner and colleagues' EMBO critique directly disputes those assumptions and the extrapolation from component proposals to comprehensive reversal. The book makes this disputed program its organizing argument, not an incidental speculation.
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage. General explanation of a biomedical research program, not specialist instruction or personal treatment advice; H3 and V7 do not apply. Bains praises its scientific stimulus while rejecting its extreme version. De Grey defends repair as engineering rather than mere treatment of symptoms. The Technology Review challenge did not prove the program unworthy of debate; that is a stronger test than V9, which does not require refutation. Criticism predates the book but concerns the same seven-part framework described in Bains's book review. The veto does not deny the value of research into aging. T11 applies to the central prevention of age-related disease and debility. Not selected.
notes: Sound molecular background is extended into uncertain claims of completeness and joint feasibility.
Connects cell damage, repair technology, funding and research priorities.
The repair-versus-prevention distinction is useful, but the global promise is unsafe as a forecast.
Explains candidate damage mechanisms and interventions, with missing validation of the whole system.
D=8, moderate confidence from Bains, the contents and the scientific review debate. Seven distinct repair problems add learning; advocacy has lower yield.
Cell biology has durable value; proposed interventions and timelines need updating.
Biotechnology and engineering strategy fit, with disease dominating.
Scientifically informed authors; substantial specialist disagreement about the central program.
Clear analogies help explain complex material; campaigning interrupts the explanation.
Accessible but sometimes immoderate polemical language.

title: Ages of Discord: A Structural-Demographic Analysis of American History
author: Peter Turchin
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage. Main purpose is explanatory historical modeling, not teaching mathematical proficiency; H3 does not apply. Richerson praises dynamic models but notes imperfect proxies, informal graphical fit and the difficulty of separating cycles from major shocks. These are material limitations, yet the inspected specialist review supports the research program and does not establish a high-confidence foundational veto. Not treated as a validated exact forecast. T11 for US history and T12 for political instability. Not selected for the approachable-narrative quota because of its academic presentation and unresolved model validation.
notes: Explicit models and proxies enable scrutiny; observational fit cannot by itself identify causes.
Integrates wages, demography, elite competition, state finances and instability.
Useful framework for comparing structural pressures, with substantial transfer uncertainty.
Feedback models make proposed mechanisms explicit, without fully separating rival explanations.
D=8, moderate confidence from Richerson's detailed review and readers. Proxy construction and contrasting periods provide substantial learning; background theory recurs.
The modeling questions endure more than a particular crisis forecast.
Quantification and institutional risk fit, but production and technology are secondary.
Relevant quantitative scholarship and serious specialist engagement, without consensus validation.
Data-heavy and academically organized; less approachable than narrative history.
Generally explicit variables and limitations, with some overconfident broad inference.

title: The Listening Society: A Metamodern Guide to Politics, Book One
author: Hanzi Freinacht
note: Mandatory Karpathy coverage. Popular political philosophy, not technical instruction or routine relationship advice. Inspected author-hosted chapter extracts propose welfare reform and explicitly acknowledge coercion risks and democratic safeguards. Activist language alone does not establish V6, nor is reform advocacy sufficient for V5. Psychological development is used for social theory, not primarily a personal support program. Reader criticism raises ideological asymmetry, but inspected evidence is insufficient for a confident serious veto. Low confidence retained; not selected despite high reader rating because independent specialist validation was not established.
notes: Broad developmental claims outrun the evidence inspected; safeguards are stated but efficacy remains uncertain.
Links psychological development, welfare institutions, technology and political culture.
Some useful questions about psychological needs, with weakly established policy transfer.
A proposed stage framework rather than well-tested causal institutional analysis.
D=5, low confidence from two chapter extracts, publisher synopsis and reader reports. Developmental distinctions add content; labels and rhetorical framing add less.
Welfare questions endure, but the new-stage framework may date.
Institutional design has partial relevance; little technical or industrial depth.
No strong independent specialist validation established in this review.
Provocative rhetoric and conceptual vocabulary obstruct an otherwise organized argument.
Sweeping labels and deliberate posturing reduce precision.
